title: Obon, the fifth time
hook: welcoming ancestors, and those you've lost these five years
tomorrow: the woman who raised him wove him a cloth. why give it away?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Asalha: the first sermon's full moon, and monks who stopped walking for the rains. The wheel still turns. Now the season's other door, the one the dead come through.

A plate of fruit beside an old photo, a small fire at the door at dusk: at Obon in Japan, families light welcome fires so the dead can find their way back to the old house. They come home. At Vu Lan, a Vietnamese festival from the same root, something odder can happen at the temple door. At some temples, someone pins a rose on your shirt. A red one if your mother is living. A white one if she has died. A festival of the dead, and red roses for the living. Why?
screen: `A FIRE AT THE DOOR.` → `A ROSE ON YOUR SHIRT.` → `RED FOR LIVING, WHITE FOR GONE.` → `WHY THE LIVING?`

segments.voice: Both festivals come from the Ullambana Sutra, a Chinese Buddhist scripture. The first half is the part people retell. Moggallana finds his mother among the hungry ghosts, starving. The food he brings her bursts into flame before she can eat it. The Buddha tells him to make offerings, as the rains retreat ends, to the whole community of monks, and the gift given in her name frees her. The puzzle's answer sits in the second half, which is easy to skip. Moggallana, grateful, asks a question for everyone after him: can people in the future do this for their parents too? Yes, the Buddha says, and he names both kinds: parents still living, for long life and health, and parents who have died, for release from suffering. So the sutra was never only about the dead. It's about the people you owe your life to, on both sides of that line. That's the teaching under both festivals: gratitude to parents, and merit given in someone's name, shared with the living and the dead. The roses aren't in the sutra; they're credited to a short essay by the Vietnamese monk Thich Nhat Hanh, about wearing a flower for your mother. The lamps and the welcome fires say the other half. The ones who are gone are invited, not only mourned. Obon sets a place for them, and gives in their name.
screen: `THE FOOD BURSTS INTO FLAME.` · `GIVE TO THE WHOLE COMMUNITY.` · `PARENTS LIVING, PARENTS GONE.` · `THE GONE ARE INVITED, NOT ONLY MOURNED.` · then, large: `THEY COME HOME.`

segments.voice: If you can, light a candle or a small lamp; if not, rest your eyes on any light in the room. For each person you've lost, these five years or long ago, let the flame hold their name for one breath. When the names run out, keep looking at the light, and let it be a welcome.
Obon: the days when the dead are welcomed home with fires and lanterns, from the Ullambana Sutra.
Your line: they come home, and the living get a flower too. Three of seven, lit.

howItsDone: At Obon, Japanese families clean graves, set food and flowers at the home altar, light welcome and farewell fires, and dance the Bon Odori; at Vu Lan, Vietnamese Buddhists give to temples in their parents' names, and at some temples people wear a red or white rose.

sources.ref: Ullambana Sutra (Moggallana's mother among the hungry ghosts; the offering at the end of the rains; the question for future disciples and their parents, living and dead)
Thich Nhat Hanh, 'A Rose for Your Pocket' (the essay behind the rose custom at Vu Lan)

notes: Ullambana Sutra paraphrased: Moggallana's food turns to flame; the Buddha says the combined power of the assembled Sangha is needed and sets the offering on the day the rains retreat ends; Moggallana then asks whether future disciples may make the offering for their parents, and the Buddha names present parents (long life, without illness) and parents of past generations (release from suffering). The sutra's 'seven generations' is left out to avoid a number. Confirm.

Rose custom at Vu Lan (red if your mother is living, white if she has died) attributed to Thich Nhat Hanh's essay 'A Rose for Your Pocket'; stated as 'at some temples' in howItsDone. Confirm the attribution and wording.
Trapdoor floor 3: 'no Pali counterpart' and 'a Chinese scripture' — confirm the scholarly framing.
For parents: the hungry-ghost image (food bursting into flame) is told in one plain line; the practice invites remembering people who have died.

Shape: puzzle (why does a festival of the dead pin roses on the living?). Mai's arc: Ông lights lamps for his parents at the altar in his new room; Mai's mom Linh is reminded that Vu Lan is for living parents too.
